A.question: What NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO clinical practice guideline recommendations or clinical trial evidence address targeted therapy for TP53 alterations in cancer? Cite the specific guideline or trial.
A.text:
7ef4", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching published medical literature, guidelines, FDA, CDC, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}, {"callid": "5afd2bdb-af29-4232-9c05-b390b6521cf9", "kind": "search", "label": "Searching full-text sources from NEJM, JAMA, Nature, NCCN, Cochrane, Wiley, and more", "id": "searchmedicalliterature", "active": true, "children": [], "paragraphindex": 0, "metadata": {}, "queries": []}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query, searched for evidence"}


No targeted agent is currently approved or endorsed by NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO specifically to treat TP53-altered cancer, and no drug directly targeting mutant p53 has achieved regulatory approval in any tumor type.[[1]] Across guidelines, TP53 status functions primarily as a prognostic/risk-stratification biomarker rather than a therapeutic target, and the consistent guideline-level recommendation—most explicit in myeloid neoplasms—is preferential enrollment in clinical trials because standard therapies perform poorly.[[2]][[3]][[4]] All direct p53-targeting strategies remain investigational.
NCCN guideline recommendations (myeloid neoplasms)
The clearest guideline statements addressing TP53 come from the NCCN AML and MDS guidelines, where TP53 defines an adverse-risk entity and steers patients toward trials rather than a specific targeted drug:
- AML: TP53 mutation (VAF ≥10%, mono- or biallelic) is classified as poor/adverse risk per the ELN stratification adopted by NCCN. The guideline states outcomes with conventional induction remain poor and the panel prioritizes cl[[2]]inical trial enrollment; off-trial, less-intensive chemotherapy is preferred over intensive induction for most patients not on a trial.
- MDS: NCCN notes that patients with TP53 mutations—particularly biallelic—have a poor prognosis even with allogeneic transplant, that such cases should be discussed with a transplant physician, and that patients should be enrolled in a clinical trial whenever possible.[[3]]
The NCCN AML adverse-risk table is shown below, including the footnote defining the TP53 threshold:
[[2]]
The emerging/targeted strategies under investigation for TP53-mutated AML/MDS (HMA ± venetoclax backbone plus p53 reactivators or immune agents) are summarized in this schematic:
[[5]]
No TP53-specific recommendation in solid-tumor guidelines
The retrieved NCCN, ASCO, and ESMO solid-tumor guidance does not recommend a TP53-directed targeted therapy. The one germline-focused NCCN reference (Genetic/Familial High-Risk Assessment) addresses interpreting germline TP53 P/LP variants and [Li-Fraumeni syndrome](/rare-disease/li-fraumeni-syndrome)—distinguishing true germline findings from CHIP/somatic confounders—rather than targeted treatment.[[6]] No ESMO document recommending a TP53-targeted agent was identified in the retrieved literature.
Clinical trial evidence by strategy
Mutant-p53 reactivators (small molecules restoring wild-type conformation):
- Eprenetapopt (APR-246) is the most clinically advanced. A phase Ib/II trial of eprenetapopt + azacitidine in TP53-mutant MDS/AML produced an ORR of 71% with 44% CR. However, the phase 3 trial in TP53-mutant M[[7]][[8]]DS (NCT03745716) failed its primary CR endpoint (33.3% vs 22.4% with azacitidine alone, P≈0.13), ending its development in this indication. It has also been studied as post-transplant maintenance and with venetoclax/pembrolizumab.[[1]][[9]][[10]]
- Rezatapopt (PC14586), a Y220C-selective reactivator, showed preliminary efficacy and acceptable safety in phase 1 and is in a phase 2 basket trial for TP53 Y220C solid tumors (NCT04585750), including a combination with pembrolizumab.[[11]][[12]][[13]]
- Arsenic trioxide (ATO) reactivates structural p53 mutants; the first-in-human PANDA-T0 pilot trial (NCT03855371) of ATO + decitabine in p53-structural-mutant AML/MDS achieved marrow CR in 4 of 5 patients.[[13]][[14]]
- Earlier/other reactivators (COTI-2, PRIMA-1) remain in early-phase testing.[[15]][[16]][[17]]
MDM2 inhibition (relevant to TP53 wild-type/functional tumors):
- Idasanutlin was tested in the phase 3 MIRROS trial (idasanutlin + cytarabine in relapsed/refractory AML, enrolled regardless of TP53 status); the idasanutlin + venetoclax combination showed minimal activity in TP53-mutant disease (3/10 ORR, no CRs). MDM2 antagonists (e[[15]][[18]].g., alrizomadlin/APG-115) are being tested with pembrolizumab in solid tumors.[[12]]
Synthetic-lethal/DNA-damage-response approaches (exploiting loss of the G1/S checkpoint):
- The WEE1 inhibitor adavosertib (AZD1775) has been studied with TP53 stratification; the randomized phase 2 FOCUS4-C trial showed improved PFS in RAS/TP53-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer, and adavosertib + carboplatin enhanced efficacy in TP53-mutated ovarian cancer (at a cost of hematologic toxicity).[[19]]
- ATR/CHK1, XPO1, and HDAC/antiangiogenic combinations (e.g., pazopanib + vorinostat in TP53-hotspot-mutant solid tumors, NCT01339871) have early-phase support.[[19]][[20]][[21]]
Immune-based approaches: TP53-mutated tumors may associate with higher TMB/PD-L1 in some contexts, and ICIs (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, sabatolimab/anti-TIM-3) are being tested in TP53-mutant AML/MDS and selected solid tumors, with variable activity.[[18]][[22]]
The range of mechanistic strategies and the specific compound–residue interactions are depicted here:
[[23]]
Given that guidelines explicitly prioritize trial enrollment for TP53-altered myeloid disease, the following search identifies currently recruiting options.

The search returned 10 available trials, though most are molecularly-guided basket or precision-oncology registry studies rather than dedicated TP53-targeted protocols. Among the top trials in the search results above, [NCT03089554](/clinical-trials/NCT03089554) (genomic testing to assign targeted therapy) and the MD Anderson personalized cancer therapy program ([NCT01772771](/clinical-trials/NCT01772771)) can route TP53-altered patients to matched agents, and [NCT04169737](/clinical-trials/NCT04169737) evaluates acalabrutinib + venetoclax in high-risk CLL/SLL (a population enriched for TP53 aberration). Dedicated TP53-reactivator trials such as the rezatapopt Y220C study (NCT04585750) were not surfaced here and would need a Y220C-specific or solid-tumor search.

No NCCN, ASCO, or ESMO guideline currently recommends a TP53-directed targeted agent as standard of care in any cancer, and no p53-targeting drug has regulatory approval. TP53 is guideline-actionable almost entirely as a negative predictive and prognostic biomarker — it redirects patients away from DNA-damaging therapy and toward targeted agents, transplant, or clinical trials — and, in the germline setting, toward intensive surveillance and radiation avoidance. The one exception in development is rezatapopt (PC14586), an allele-selective reactivator of p53 Y220C, which produced the first prospective evidence of direct pharmacologic p53 targeting in the PYNNACLE phase 1 trial.[[1]]
Rezatapopt — the only direct p53-targeted agent with clinical efficacy data
- PYNNACLE phase 1 (NEJM 2026): 77 heavily pretreated patients with locally advanced/metastatic TP53 Y220C–mutated solid tumors. Investigator-assessed and blinded central review ORR both 20% (14/71 evaluable), with 2 complete responses; confirmed responses in ovarian (7), breast (3), and one each endometrial, head and neck, prostate, and [small cell lung cancer](/rare-disease/small-cell-lung-cancer). Median DOR 7.0 months (95% CI 2.8–10.6), median PFS 4.3 months, median OS 11.4 months.[[1]]
- KRAS co-mutation abolished activity: all 14 responders were KRAS wild-type, and no response occurred in tumors with both TP53 Y220C and a KRAS single-nucleotide variant. In the Y220C/KRAS–wild-type population treated within the efficacious dose range, ORR was 30% (14/46).[[1]]
- Recommended phase 2 dose: 2000 mg orally once daily with food; nausea and vomiting were the most common treatment-related adverse events, and administration with food reduced GI toxicity and pharmacokinetic variability. ctDNA Y220C variant allele frequency fell in 95% of assessable patients, supporting on-target activity.[[1]]
- The registrational phase 2 PYNNACLE study (NCT04585750) restricts enrollment to TP53 Y220C with wild-type KRAS and has not reported. Y220C accounts for ro[[1]][[2]]ughly 1.8% of TP53 mutations.[[3]]
- Acquired resistance is on-target: ctDNA, biopsy, and rapid-autopsy profiling at progression showed secondary TP53 alterations in cis with Y220C — DNA-binding-domain or truncating mutations that abolish transcriptional activity, and mutations within the drug-binding surface.[[4]]
A 20–30% response rate in a phase 1 population does not establish clinical benefit; access should be through trial enrollment.
Phase 3 failures that should close off other p53-directed approaches
- Eprenetapopt (APR-246) + azacitidine: phase Ib/II in TP53-mutant MDS/oligoblastic AML gave ORR 71% and CR 44%, but the randomized phase 3 in TP53-mutant MDS missed its primary endpoint (CR 33.3% vs 22.4% with azacitidine alone, P = .13).[[5]][[6]][[7]]
- Magrolimab (anti-CD47): ENHANCE-2 in untreated TP53-mutated AML was stopped for futility — median OS 4.4 vs 6.6 months in the non-intensive arm (HR 1.132) and 7.3 vs 11.1 months in the intensive arm. ENHANCE in higher-risk MDS was negative (CR 21.3% vs 23.6%; median OS 15.9 vs 18.6 months, HR 1.203) with more grade ≥3, serious, and fatal adverse events on magrolimab. ENHANCE-3 was terminated early for futility and excess deaths. Other anti-CD47 programs (evor[[8]][[9]][[10]][[11]]pacept) have also been terminated.[[12]]
- WEE1 inhibition (synthetic lethality with G1/S checkpoint loss): FOCUS4-C randomized adavosertib vs active monitoring in RAS/TP53-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer — PFS 3.61 vs 1.87 months (HR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18–0.68, P = .0022) with no OS benefit (14.0 vs 12.8 months); benefit concentrated in left-sided tumors and KRAS codon 12/13. This remains the strongest randomized signal for a TP53-mutation-selected strategy in solid tumors, but it is not guideline-recommended, and TP53 mutation alone is not a validated predictive biomarker for WEE1 inhibition — cyclin E1/CCNE1 status appears more predictive.[[13]][[14]]
Where NCCN guidelines make TP53 status change management
